What's in the way

The gaps

None of these are talent problems. They're system problems, and every one of them is fixable.

  • "I'm versatile"It's true, and it's your gift. But a new listener needs one clear first impression before they'll follow you into everything else. Lead with one lane, explore later.
  • Three covers, three worldsPrada is a script logo on a photo, L3zzY is gold glitter with a jet and cash, 3s Back is a cartoon in a template. Someone scrolling can't tell they're the same artist.
  • The six-week drop-offYou said it yourself: you go hard for about a month and a half, then life pulls you away. The algorithm and the audience both forget fast.
  • Editing bottleneckYou're capturing more than anyone can cut in iMovie. Every hour you spend editing is an hour you're not making music.
  • No home baseInstagram is rented land. Your merch, a documentary and the full catalog need a place you own.
  • Quick fixes on the profileYour courtside profile photo fits the story; just make sure your face reads at thumbnail size. The pinned post is too dark, with your face half covered. The bio is a raw Spotify link.

A first look · Direction B

Number 3

This one comes from somewhere else: the fifteen years you spent as an athlete. You put the ball down for music, but the number never left you. Here, the 3 is a jersey number, and every release is a new season.

Why this could work

It's a story nobody else in party R&B can tell. It explains the discipline, the tough love and the coaching mindset without you saying a word. And sports graphics are built to look the same every time, which is exactly the consistency you said you struggle with.

The mark

Your hand logo in team colors, a collegiate block 3 built like a jersey number, and a team patch for hats, merch and the end of every video.

Black and white, red on top

Every photo goes high-contrast black and white with heavy grain, like a game-day photo in a newspaper. Red never touches the photo. It only shows up in the graphics, so it hits harder.

The roadmap

Four phases to the next level

Each phase builds on the one before. Don't skip ahead.

1
NOW → END OF OCTOBER

Lock in

  • Run the Halloween drop all month with your six videos. Post on a schedule, not on a feeling.
  • Keep the courtside profile photo or swap in a tighter shot, as long as your face reads at thumbnail size.
  • Swap the pinned post for something bright where we can see your face.
  • Rewrite the bio: who you are in one line, plus a link hub instead of a raw track link.
  • Get on the Coke Studio list now, so you're in the first wave when the rebuilt studio opens in February.

Goal: a page that tells a stranger who L3 is in three seconds.

2
NOVEMBER → DECEMBER

Build the system

  • Design the L3 visual identity: one mark, one type style, one color story, one cover template.
  • Get an editor. Cheap and fast for social cuts; save your own time for the hero pieces.
  • Set up scheduled posting so the work keeps going out on the weeks you're with your boys.
  • Launch a simple website: music, videos, story, and later the documentary.
  • Start filming the documentary now. Capture everything; cut it later.
  • Plan the Coke Studio day: the songs, the looks, the set, the crew.

Goal: consistency that doesn't depend on you having a good week.

3
JANUARY → MARCH

Coke Studio and the real rollout

  • Pick the strongest party R&B single and give it a six-week lead-up: teasers, snippets, behind-the-scenes, release.
  • Shoot the Coke Studio session in February, in the rebuilt room. Make it the launch moment for the new L3.
  • Use that footage as the anchor content for the whole rollout.
  • Book live dates and film every one. Shows are content.
  • Start light PR: playlists, blogs, local radio, podcasts.

Goal: one record that people outside your circle know is yours.

4
SPRING 2027 →

Scale it

  • Release a full project built in one lane, with one look, on a real plan.
  • Release the documentary on your site, cut into clips for social.
  • Launch the motivation side: a series or podcast where you talk straight to women about knowing their worth.
  • Bring on a manager. With momentum behind you, you'll attract a better one.

Goal: a brand bigger than any one song.

Fixing the six-week drop-off

The weekly rhythm

Put this on your big paper calendar. It's built so it still runs on your busy weeks.

DayWhat happensWho

TuesdayPost 1: a music moment. Song snippet, studio clip or performance.Scheduled

Coke Studio

Making the session count

The studio is closed for a rebuild and reopens around February with more cameras in every room. That gives you three months to show up ready. You get the room and the logo; Coke doesn't promote it for you, so the plan around the session is what makes it worth anything.

Bring your people

You build beats on the spot and work fast. Bring your own producer-engineer so the house engineer doesn't slow your rhythm.

Shoot like a campaign

Two camera guys plus the room's locked-off cameras. One live-streams, one shoots stills and BTS. Plan the outfits as looks, not just changes.

Set the room

Dim the lights, wash it in red, put your L3 mark on the big LED screen. It should look like your world, not a borrowed studio.

Plan the after

Before you walk in, know what gets posted when. One session should feed a month of content.
